lis-01.title: Information and Libraries
explain: Every day we look for things, read them, and judge them many times over. The discipline that studies this process is **library and information science**. It studies how information is created, organized, found, and used, and it works to support that flow.

First, the terms. **Data** are individual records that have no context attached yet. **Information** is data with context added, so that we can tell what it means. **Knowledge** is information that has been connected with understanding and made one's own. The boundaries are not cut as sharply as with a knife, but dividing things into these three levels helps organize our thinking.

A **library** is a place that gathers information and makes it available to those who need it. Its work is usually divided into four parts.
- **Collection**: acquiring materials by purchase or donation
- **Organization**: classifying materials and building catalogs so they can be found
- **Preservation**: storing and repairing materials safely so that they last
- **Provision**: helping users read and borrow materials

Libraries are classified by the users they serve. Examples are public libraries for local residents, school libraries for members of a school, academic libraries that support the learning and research of a university community, special libraries focused on a particular field or institution, and national libraries that collect and preserve a country's publications.

There is also the flow of the person who uses information. They notice what they are curious about (an information need), look for materials, weigh whether what they found is trustworthy, and use it. The following lessons in this department trace this flow step by step.

lis-02.title: Classification
explain: How do we find a wanted book among hundreds of thousands? We group similar things together and place them in a fixed order. This work is **classification**. Libraries most commonly use **subject classification**, which groups books by the **subject** they treat. As a result, books on the same subject stand side by side on the shelf.

A table that turns subjects into agreed-upon symbols is a **classification scheme**. A classification scheme is a **hierarchy** that descends from large classes to small ones. Often the notation becomes longer with each step down. Real libraries widely use numeric schemes such as the Korean Decimal Classification and the Dewey Decimal Classification. In this lesson we use a fictional scheme to see the principle.

A book occupies only one place on the shelf, so each book is given one class number. If a book spans several subjects, we choose the one with the greatest weight. The criterion here is not the **words in the title** or the **form of the book**, but **what the book is about**.
On the spine, a **call number**, made of the class number plus symbols such as one for the author, tells the location on the shelf.

lis-03.title: Catalogs and Metadata
explain: We cannot search the shelves book by book. So libraries make a **catalog**, a record of the materials they hold. Each record in the catalog is like a small card describing one item.

Data that describe an item in this way are called **metadata**: "data about data." A book's title, author, and year of publication are not the text of the book but metadata that describe it. The shooting date and file size of a digital photo are the same kind of thing.

Elements that often appear in a catalog record are as follows.
- **Title**: the name of the item
- **Author**: the person who created the content
- **Publication information**: the publisher, year of publication, and so on
- **Subject terms**: words that express the content
- **Class number**: a symbol that tells the place on the shelf
- **Standard number**: a number given to each book individually, such as the International Standard Book Number (ISBN)
The elements a user enters when looking for an item are called **access points**. Title, author, and subject terms are typical ones.

Subject terms in particular must be consistent. If one record writes 'avian' and another writes 'bird' for the same concept, the search results split in two. So libraries keep a **controlled vocabulary**, which uses one fixed term for each concept, and guide users to the fixed term even when they search with another word.

lis-04.title: Searching
explain: Looking for items in catalogs and databases is **searching**. Rather than typing a whole sentence into the box, it usually works better to pull out the core words, that is, **keywords**. From what you wonder about, pick two or three core concepts, and for each concept think of other words with the same meaning (synonyms) and of broader or narrower words.

The rules for combining keywords logically are **Boolean operators**.
- **AND**: keeps only records that contain both words. Conditions increase, so the results **decrease**
- **OR**: keeps records that contain either one. The results **increase**. It is used to join synonyms
- **NOT**: removes records that contain the word that follows
How operators are used and which characters are used for them differ somewhat from one search system to another. Here we learn only the concepts.

If there are too many results, add conditions with AND or switch to more specific words; if there are too few, add synonyms with OR or switch to broader words. It is rare for a first search statement to be right at once, so we revise it as we look at the results.

lis-05.title: Evaluating Information
explain: Not everything that turns up in a search is trustworthy. In an environment where anyone can post, **weighing is as important as finding**. A high ranking in the results, or being widely shared, is not evidence of trustworthiness. Rankings can be decided for reasons other than accuracy.

There are four questions often used to weigh a source. They are not an absolute scorecard but questions that guide thinking.
- **Author**: who wrote it, and do they know the field?
- **Evidence**: are the grounds and sources of the claims stated?
- **Date**: when was it written, and is it still correct? This matters more in fast-changing fields
- **Purpose**: why was it made? To inform, or to persuade or sell?

We also distinguish the nature of the material. A **primary source** is a record made by someone who directly experienced an event, or one produced in that period. Diaries, letters, and photographs from the time are examples. A **secondary source** is a text that interprets and explains on the basis of primary sources and the like. Neither is better in itself; their uses differ depending on what one wants to know.

When you meet an unfamiliar site, do not read only its own "About" page; leave the site and look up how other trustworthy sources evaluate it. This is called **lateral reading**. This is because anyone can write well of themselves.

lis-06.title: Information Ethics
explain: Once you have found and sifted information, the last step is **using** it. The agreements to be observed when using information made by others are **information ethics**. This lesson introduces general principles and is not legal advice. Rules differ by country and institution, so in real situations you should follow the guidance of the institution concerned.

**Citation** is bringing in another person's writing or ideas and using them while stating the source. When copying text exactly, set it off from your own writing with quotation marks or the like, and give information that lets readers find the original, such as author, title, year of publication, and page number. **Plagiarism** is using another person's expression or ideas as one's own without stating the source.

There is a common misunderstanding. It is easy to think that changing a few words or summarizing in your own words removes the need for a source. But even if the wording changes, **if you took the idea, you must state the source**. Conversely, widely known common knowledge often does not need a source each time.

**Copyright** is the right a creator holds over the use of their own creation. As a general principle, what is protected is the created **expression**. No one can monopolize facts or ideas themselves. So writing the same fact anew in your own expression is possible, but copying another person's sentences as they are may require permission or a defined exception.
A library must respect the rights of creators and the personal information of users while giving users access to information. People who use information must strike the same balance.

examples.title: The same paragraph, two uses
body: Suppose a fictional book has the sentence "Tidal flats are home to countless organisms and also a resting place for migratory birds."

Plagiarism: changing this sentence to "Tidal flats are the habitat of many organisms and a place where migratory birds stop to rest" and placing it in my writing without a source. Only the wording was changed; the content and flow of another person's writing were taken as they are.

Legitimate use: stating the source and using only as much as my argument needs, as in "An explanation exists that tidal flats are where migratory birds stop to rest (Fictional Author, Stories of the Tidal Flat, 2018, p. 12)."

lis-07.title: The Structure of Decimal Classification: DDC and KDC
explain: Suppose a library has a hundred thousand books. If books are placed in the order they arrive, books on the same subject end up scattered, and users must scan the shelves from beginning to end. As we learned in Stage 1, grouping by subject and fixing an order turns the shelves into a map. This lesson takes apart, layer by layer, the structure of the most widely used tool for making that map, decimal classification.

There are broadly two ways of building a classification scheme. In **enumerative classification**, the designer **lists in advance** the possible subjects, and one finds where a book falls among them. In **analytico-synthetic classification**, the elements that make up a subject are defined separately and the notation is made by **combining** them when needed; this is treated in the next lesson. The Dewey Decimal Classification (DDC) and the Korean Decimal Classification (KDC) are basically enumerative, with some auxiliary tables adding a synthetic character.
Decimal classification first divides all of knowledge into **ten main classes**. The main classes of the KDC are as follows.

- 000 General works
- 100 Philosophy
- 200 Religion
- 300 Social sciences
- 400 Natural sciences
- 500 Technology
- 600 Arts
- 700 Language
- 800 Literature
- 900 History

The DDC shares the idea of dividing the main classes into ten, but the arrangement is a little different. For example, in the DDC the 400s are language, the 500s natural sciences, the 600s technology, and the 700s the arts. The same number can mean a different subject depending on the country and the scheme, so when speaking of a number one must state which scheme it belongs to.

Each main class is divided again into ten **divisions**, and each division into ten **sections**. In a three-digit notation, the first digit indicates the main class, the second the division, and the third the section. To narrow further, digits are added after the decimal point, and every additional digit splits the subject into ten branches. The longer the digits, the narrower and more specific the subject. Within one main class there are 10 × 10 = 100 sections, and if one writes one digit after the decimal point there are in theory 1000 branches.

On the shelf, notations are arranged not as integers but **compared from the leading digit, like decimals**. 330.15 comes before 330.2, because 330.2 read as 330.20 comes after 330.15. A common mistake is thinking that a longer string means a larger value. Because a book is given one notation, a book spanning several subjects follows the subject with the greatest weight, and is not decided by the words of its title alone. **Auxiliary tables** that express form or region are sometimes attached after the main notation to subdivide further.

The weaknesses of enumeration are also clear. Since it reflects the academic landscape at the time the scheme was made, a newly emerging field may lack a fitting place, and a subject spanning several disciplines is placed in only one spot, making it hard to find from other viewpoints. So classification schemes are revised periodically, and even for the same subject the number may differ by edition. The explanation in this lesson is for understanding the structure; actual numbers must be checked in the latest edition of the scheme.

examples.title: Identifying the main class
body: Conditions (three fictional books): Where Stars Are Born is a popular science book explaining how stars form; First Steps in Circuit Design introduces how to design electronic circuits; The Sound System of Korean treats the rules of Korean pronunciation.
Step 1: Write in one line what each book is about. Star formation is a celestial phenomenon, circuit design is engineering technology, and Korean pronunciation is the system of one language.

Step 2: Map to the KDC main classes. The first book is 400 Natural sciences, the second 500 Technology, the third 700 Language. The third book is written in Korean but is not a literary work, so it is not 800. Interpretation: the criterion of classification is not the language or form of the book but the subject it treats.

examples.title: Lining up decimal notations
body: Conditions: The notations to be placed on the shelf are 330.1, 330.15, 329.9, 330.2, and 331.
Step 1: Compare the integer parts. 329.9 is first and 331 is last. The other three have the same integer part, 330.

Step 2: Within 330, compare the digits after the decimal point from the leading digit. .1, .15, and .2 read as 0.10, 0.15, and 0.20, so the order is 330.1, 330.15, 330.2. The final arrangement is 329.9, 330.1, 330.15, 330.2, 331. Interpretation: reading 330.15 as "three hundred thirty point fifteen" and placing it after 330.2 is the typical error.

checks.prompt: Match each KDC main class number with its name.
checks.hint: From 000, in steps of 100: general works, philosophy, religion, social sciences.
checks.explanation: In the KDC, 300 is social sciences, 500 technology, 700 language, and 900 history. In the DDC, 400 is language and 500 is natural sciences, so the arrangement differs.

checks.prompt: One division (for example, the 330s) is split into 10 sections, and each section is split into 10 further branches by one digit after the decimal point. In theory, how many notations can be written within this division, up to one digit after the decimal point?

lis-08.title: Analytico-Synthetic Classification and Facets
explain: To organize a book with many intertwined elements, such as "controlling pests and diseases on tomato leaves grown on a Seoul rooftop," with an enumerative scheme, the scheme would already have to list that subject. But with only a few more elements, the possible combinations explode and cannot all be written in the table. To get past this limit, a method arose that first defines the **viewpoints from which a subject is divided**.

One viewpoint that makes up a subject is called a **facet**. The Indian librarian Ranganathan, in his Colon Classification, popularized analyzing a compound subject into facets and building the notation by joining the terms chosen from each facet. This is **analytico-synthetic classification**. The table lists only terms by facet, and the combinations are made when needed.
The basic framework Ranganathan presented has five facets.

- **Personality**: the central object of the subject
- **Matter**: the material or composition of the object
- **Energy**: the activity or process that takes place
- **Space**: the place
- **Time**: the period
Taking the initials of these five facets gives the name PMEST. This framework is not a law that fits every subject perfectly but a guide to aid analysis.

explain.alt: A table of five rows. The title above reads "A fictional book: Controlling pests and diseases on tomato leaves on a Seoul rooftop." In each row, the name in the left cell is joined by an arrow to the word in the right cell. Personality is tomato, Matter is leaf, Energy is pest and disease control, Space is Seoul rooftop, Time is the 2020s.

explain: The figure shows the result of analyzing a fictional book by facets. The words of the title are not all treated at the same level; they are divided into object (tomato), material (leaf), activity (pest and disease control), and place (Seoul rooftop), and the period (the 2020s), which is not in the title, is also recorded as a facet. The order of analysis is to pick words from the book, decide which facet each word belongs to, and choose the term for each facet from the table.

Calculating the number of combinations shows the efficiency of this method. If the five facets have 6, 4, 5, 3, and 4 defined terms respectively, the terms to write in the table number 6 + 4 + 5 + 3 + 4 = 22. Yet the possible synthesized subjects number 6 × 4 × 5 × 3 × 4 = 1440, and an enumerative scheme would have to create all 1440 places in advance.

When making a synthesized notation, one must fix the **citation order** in which facets are placed. This is because the shelf is one-dimensional, so the facet placed first becomes the first criterion for gathering the same books. If Space is placed first, books about the same region gather in one place and are then divided by object within it. If the object is placed first, books on the same object gather regardless of region. There are limits too. Dividing into facets depends on the analyst's training (whether pest and disease control is seen as Energy or as an object may differ from person to person), and a single shelf order can hold only a single citation order. The filter search of online catalogs is a modern application that lets us escape this one-dimensional constraint.

Step 2: Assign them to facets. Personality is pottery, Matter is glaze, Energy is making, Space is the village workshop in Gwangju, and Time is the 1990s. lis-09.title: Bibliographic Models and Cataloging Rules: FRBR, RDA, and MARC
explain: Suppose the same novel exists in a Korean edition, an English translation, and an e-book, and the library shelf holds two copies of the same edition. If the catalog records all of this as "one book," we cannot tell that a translation exists; if it records each copy separately, the fact that they are the same work is buried. This is because the unit needed differs depending on what the user is trying to do.

The International Federation of Library Associations and Institutions (IFLA) put this problem in order with **FRBR** (Functional Requirements for Bibliographic Records). It treats the user's tasks as finding, identifying, selecting, and obtaining, and divides bibliographic entities into four levels. The later IFLA LRM carries on the idea of these levels.

- **Work**: the abstract intellectual or artistic creation itself
- **Expression**: the work realized in a particular text. Each translation and each revised text is a separate expression
- **Manifestation**: an expression issued in a particular publication form. A different edition, publisher, or medium (paper or electronic) is a different manifestation
- **Item**: a single copy of a manifestation. It is an actual volume on the shelf or one file

explain.alt: A box diagram with four levels. In the top "Work" level there is a box "Song of the Moonlit Garden" (a fictional novel). In the "Expression" level there are boxes "Korean original text" and "English translation text." In the "Manifestation" level there are boxes "2015 hardcover" (Korean), "2020 e-book" (Korean), and "2022 paperback" (English). In the "Item" level there are boxes "2 copies held," "1 file," and "2 copies held" respectively. Lines run from the Korean original text to the first two manifestations, from the English translation text to the 2022 paperback, and from each manifestation straight down to its item.

explain: Reading the figure downward, one work splits into two expressions (original and translation), and the Korean original divides again into two manifestations (hardcover and e-book). The number of items the library holds differs for each manifestation. A person looking for the same story starts at the work level, a person choosing a book to read in English starts at the expression level, and a person getting an e-book starts at the manifestation level. Dividing into levels in this way lets the catalog show the unit suited to each user task.

**RDA** (Resource Description and Access) is a set of cataloging rules for describing resources and deciding access points on the basis of such a model. Where earlier rules mainly decided how to record by the physical form of the material, RDA emphasizes which attributes to record and which relationships (translation, adaptation, and so on) to state. The rules decide the content of the record, and what format to put that record in is a separate matter.

**MARC** (Machine-Readable Cataloging) is a format that lets computers read catalog records and libraries exchange them. A record is made of fields distinguished by three-digit numeric **tags**, and the detailed elements within a field are separated by subfield codes (written ‡ in this lesson). Commonly seen tags are as follows.

- 020 International Standard Book Number (ISBN)
- 100 Main entry, personal name
- 245 Title and statement of responsibility
- 264 Publication, distribution, and manufacture information (260 was mainly used in the past)
- 300 Physical description (number of pages, etc.)
- 650 Topical subject heading

There are limits as well. MARC is an exchange **format**, so it cannot hold a conceptual model such as FRBR as it is. This is because information on the work, expression, and manifestation is mixed into a single record. So recently, methods that keep the levels separate and link them by relationships are also being studied. Also, the records in this lesson are fictional examples, and actual input rules follow the guidelines of the institution.

Step 1: Check whether the text has changed. Only (b) changes the text (translation); (c) issues the same text in a different medium. Step 2: Map to the levels. In (a), the manifestation stays the same and only items increase. (b) is a new expression. (c) is a new manifestation of the same expression. (d) is a new work. lis-10.title: Inverted Indexes and Boolean Query Processing
explain: Suppose there are a million documents. If each query read every document from the beginning to check whether the word "garden" appears, even a single query would take a long time. Recalling the index at the back of a book shows the solution. If the pages where each word appears are arranged in advance, there is no need to read the whole book when searching.

This structure used by search systems is the **inverted index**. It turns upside down the forward relation that a document contains words, and for each word collects the numbers of the documents in which the word appears. An inverted index consists of a list of words (the **dictionary**) and a list of document numbers for each word (the **postings list**), and each postings list is kept sorted by document number.
The process of building an inverted index is as follows.

1. Collect the documents
2. Split the text into words, the units of search (tokenization)
3. Unify differences in notation (normalization): upper and lower case, inflected forms, and so on
4. For each word, gather the numbers of the documents it appears in and sort them to make the postings list

explain.alt: On the left, four documents are stacked as boxes. Document 1 is "garden plant water," document 2 is "garden cat," document 3 is "plant library," and document 4 is "garden plant cat." In the table "Inverted index (term: document numbers)" on the right are written cat: 2, 4 / garden: 1, 2, 4 / library: 3 / plant: 1, 3, 4 / water: 1.

explain: Let us check that the inverted index was built from the four documents in the figure. "Garden" appears in documents 1, 2, and 4, so garden: 1, 2, 4. The number of documents in which a word appears is called the **document frequency** (df), and the df of plant is 3. A query is processed by reading only these lists. Boolean operations become set operations on the lists. AND is the intersection of two lists, OR is the union, and NOT is the difference. For example, garden AND plant is the intersection {1, 4} of {1, 2, 4} and {1, 3, 4}.

The intersection of two sorted lists can be found by scanning each list only once with two pointers. Compare the numbers at the front of the two lists: if equal, put the number in the result and advance both by one; if different, advance only the smaller one. The amount of computation is proportional not to the total number of documents but to the lengths of the two lists, so however many documents there are, processing the shorter list first is fast.

In languages like Korean where particles and endings attach, tokenization is harder. If "도서관에서" (at the library) is indexed as a single chunk, it cannot be found by "도서관" (library), so the particle is split off by morphological analysis. Typos and synonyms are also problems. The limit is more fundamental. The result of a Boolean query has only two outcomes, matching or not, so it has **no ranking**. Using many ANDs easily gives zero results, and using many ORs pours out thousands. To make up for this, models arose that give words weights and rank documents by score.

Step 1: Process the inside of the parentheses first. The union of plant {1, 3, 4} and cat {2, 4} is {1, 2, 3, 4}.
Step 2: Take the intersection with garden {1, 2, 4}. The result is {1, 2, 4}, 3 documents. Interpretation: document 3 is "plant library" and has no garden, so it was filtered out.

body: Conditions: Find the intersection of plant {1, 3, 4} and garden {1, 2, 4} with two pointers.
Step 1: Compare 1 and 1; they are equal, so put 1 in the result and advance both. Compare 3 and 2; 3 is larger, so advance only the garden side.

Step 2: Compare 3 and 4 and advance only the plant side, then compare 4 and 4; they are equal, so put 4 in the result. There are 4 comparisons in all, and the result is {1, 4}. Interpretation: each list was scanned only once, so the amount of computation is proportional to the list lengths.

lis-11.title: TF-IDF and the Vector Space Model
explain: A Boolean query only separates matching documents from non-matching ones; it does not say which of the matching documents is more suitable. The number of documents a person can read is limited, so showing them in a suitable order is important. To rank, we need a way to express numerically how well a word represents the subject of a document.

The first intuition is this. The more often a word appears in a document, the more closely related the document is to it. This value is called **term frequency** (tf). But words like "the" and "and" appear often in almost every document without distinguishing subjects. So a second intuition is needed. A word that appears in fewer documents has greater discriminating power.

Let N be the total number of documents and df the number of documents in which a word appears (document frequency). The **inverse document frequency**, which expresses discriminating power, is defined as follows. $$\mathrm{idf} = \log_{10}\frac{N}{\mathrm{df}}$$ 모든 문서에 나오는 낱말은 df = N이므로 idf = 0이 되어 가중치가 사라진다. 로그를 쓰는 이유는 희귀함의 차이가 너무 커지지 않게 눌러 주기 위해서다. 두 직관을 곱한 것이 **TF-IDF 가중치**다. $$w = \mathrm{tf} \times \mathrm{idf}$$ (Meaning of the Korean sentence between the two formulas: a word that appears in every document has df = N, so idf = 0 and its weight vanishes; the logarithm is used to damp the difference in rarity so that it does not grow too large; the product of the two intuitions, tf and idf, is the TF-IDF weight.)

Let us follow the calculation. Among 1000 documents, a word with df of 10 has idf = log10(1000/10) = log10(100) = 2. If this word appears 3 times in a document, its weight is 3 × 2 = 6. If df is 100, idf = 1, and even for the same 3 occurrences the weight drops to 3. A common word has a low score however often it appears, and a rare word has a high score with just a few occurrences. The base of the logarithm (10, 2, e) and the way tf is transformed differ from system to system; this lesson uses the simplest form with base 10.

Now regard a document as a list of numbers, one slot per word, that is, a **vector**. If there are only two words, a document is a point (an arrow) on a plane, and a query becomes a vector in the same way. This is the **vector space model**. How alike a query and a document are is measured by the cosine of the angle between the two arrows. $$\cos\theta = \frac{\sum q_i d_i}{\sqrt{\sum q_i^2}\,\sqrt{\sum d_i^2}}$$ The numerator is the sum of products of matching words, and the denominator divides by the lengths of the two vectors to remove the effect of length. The value is between 0 and 1, and the closer to 1, the more the directions agree.

Let us see why length correction is needed. For the query q = (1, 1), there are documents d1 = (4, 0) and d2 = (2, 2). d1 is a document in which only one word appears many times, and d2 is a document in which the two words appear evenly. If we simply multiply and add, both are 4, the same. But the cosine is 4 / (√2 × 4) ≈ 0.707 for d1 and 4 / (√2 × √8) = 1 for d2. The document whose word proportions match the query is judged more suitable.

The order in which a search system processes a query is simple. Turn the query into a vector, compute similarity with the candidate document vectors, sort by score, and show the top. The limits are also clear. Because words are treated as independent, meaning (synonyms, context) cannot be handled, and there is no device to stop the score from growing without bound as tf increases. Length correction is also needed so that a long document does not gain an advantage merely because it has many words. BM25 in the next lesson addresses these problems.

examples.title: Computing a TF-IDF weight
body: Conditions (a fictional collection): 1000 documents. The word library has df = 10, garden has df = 100, and "the" has df = 1000. Each word appears 3 times in one document.
Step 1: Find idf. library is log10(100) = 2, garden is log10(10) = 1, and "the" is log10(1) = 0.

Step 2: Multiply by tf. library is 3 × 2 = 6, garden is 3 × 1 = 3, and "the" is 3 × 0 = 0. Interpretation: even at the same frequency, the rarer the word, the higher the score, and a word that appears in every document scores 0.

examples.title: Comparing with the cosine
body: Conditions: In a space of two words (garden, cat), the query is q = (1, 1) and the documents are d1 = (4, 0) and d2 = (2, 2).
Step 1: Find the dot products. For q and d1 it is 1 × 4 + 1 × 0 = 4, and for q and d2 it is 1 × 2 + 1 × 2 = 4. The lengths are |q| = √2, |d1| = 4, and |d2| = √8 ≈ 2.83.

Step 2: Find the cosines. d1 is 4 / (1.414 × 4) ≈ 0.707, and d2 is 4 / (1.414 × 2.83) = 1. Interpretation: a document with the same word proportions as the query ranks higher than a document in which only one word appears many times.

lis-12.title: BM25 and Evaluating Retrieval Performance: Precision and Recall
explain: TF-IDF has two weaknesses. Is it reasonable for the scores of a document in which a word appears ten times and one in which it appears a hundred times to differ tenfold? And should a long document have its score raised on the grounds that it naturally has many occurrences of words? Both go against intuition. A widely used scoring function that refines these points is **BM25**.

BM25 fixes two things. First, **saturation**: as a word's count rises the score rises, but less and less, approaching an upper limit. Second, **length normalization**: if the document length dl is longer than the collection's average length avgdl, the score is cut. When a word appears f times in a document, the score for that word is as follows. $$\mathrm{IDF}\cdot\frac{f\,(k_1+1)}{f + k_1\left(1 - b + b\,\frac{\mathrm{dl}}{\mathrm{avgdl}}\right)}$$ The sum of this value over each word of the query is the score of the document. Commonly k1 is around 1.2 and b around 0.75, and these values are settings tuned to the collection.

Let us plug in values. With k1 = 1.2, b = 0.75, and a document length equal to the average, dl/avgdl = 1, so the parenthesis in the denominator is 1 - 0.75 + 0.75 = 1. For f = 1 the word part is 1 × 2.2 / (1 + 1.2) = 1.0, for f = 2 it is 4.4 / 3.2 = 1.375, for f = 3 it is 6.6 / 4.2 ≈ 1.571, and for f = 10 it is 22 / 11.2 ≈ 1.964. Even when the count becomes ten times larger the score does not even double, and the upper limit is k1 + 1 = 2.2. If the document length is twice the average, the parenthesis becomes 1 - 0.75 + 1.5 = 1.75, and the value for f = 3 drops to 6.6 / (3 + 2.1) ≈ 1.294.

To judge whether a scoring function is good, we need evaluation criteria. The two most basic values are **precision** and **recall**. Let TP be the retrieved documents that are relevant, FP the retrieved documents that are not relevant, and FN the relevant documents that were not retrieved. $$P = \frac{TP}{TP + FP},\quad R = \frac{TP}{TP + FN}$$ Precision is "the proportion of correct ones among what was found," and recall is "the proportion of what was found among the correct ones."

explain.alt: Two circles overlap inside a large rectangle. The left circle is named "20 relevant documents" and the right circle is named "25 retrieved documents." The non-overlapping part of the left circle is marked 5 (relevant only), the overlap is marked 15 (both), and the non-overlapping part of the right circle is marked 10 (retrieved only). Below the rectangle is written "70 other documents (100 in total)."

explain: Let us read the figure. Of 100 documents in all, 20 are relevant and the system returned 25. The 15 in the overlap are TP, the 10 that were only retrieved are FP, and the 5 that were only relevant are FN. So P = 15 / (15 + 10) = 0.6 and R = 15 / (15 + 5) = 0.75. To combine the two values into one, we use the harmonic mean, **F1**. $$F_1 = \frac{2PR}{P + R}$$ In this example it is 2 × 0.6 × 0.75 / 1.35 ≈ 0.667.

Precision and recall are often in a trade-off relation. Widening the results raises recall but mixes in irrelevant documents and lowers precision, and narrowing the results does the opposite. In the extreme, returning all 100 documents of the collection gives a recall of 1 but a precision of 20/100 = 0.2. Which matters more depends on the purpose. If only one specific fact is needed, precision weighs more; if prior research must be surveyed without omission, recall weighs more.

Evaluation figures are not all-powerful. Relevance must be judged by people, and values can change when the judges change. To compute recall one must know the number of relevant documents in the whole collection, which is hard to know in a large collection, so sample-based estimates are used. Also, one metric being good does not guarantee user satisfaction. All the figures in this chapter are fictional examples for practicing the concepts.

Step 2: P = 15/25 = 0.6, R = 15/20 = 0.75, and F1 = 2 × 0.6 × 0.75 / (0.6 + 0.75) ≈ 0.667. Interpretation: F1 is slightly lower than the simple average (0.675) because the harmonic mean is pulled closer to the lower value.

lis-13.title: Laws of Bibliometrics I: Lotka and Zipf
explain: As scholarship grew, so did the numbers of papers, authors, and words. The field that searches for recurring regularities in the production and use of literature using numbers is **bibliometrics**. Knowing the regularities gives a basis for judgments such as how much a library should spend on which materials, and which words a retrieval system should treat lightly.

There are three representative laws describing the distribution of literature. In this lesson we look at **Lotka's law**, which deals with the productivity of authors, and **Zipf's law**, which deals with the frequency of words; in the next lesson we look at Bradford's law, which deals with the scattering of journals. All three laws are empirical regularities observed in some set of materials, and do not mean that they hold exactly as natural laws do.

Lotka's law says that the number of authors who have written n papers in a field is roughly proportional to $\frac{1}{n^2}$. If the number of authors who wrote only one paper is $y_1$, the number of authors who wrote n papers is as follows. $$y_n = \frac{y_1}{n^2}$$ For example, if 400 authors wrote only one paper, then 400/4 = 100 authors wrote two, 400/9 ≈ 44 wrote three, and 400/16 = 25 wrote four. A few prolific authors write a considerable part of the papers while the majority write only one or two.

Zipf's law is a rule about words. In a body of text, line up the words in order of how often they appear and call the rank r; the frequency is then nearly inversely proportional to the rank. $$f(r) = \frac{C}{r},\quad r \cdot f(r) \approx C$$ If the word of rank 1 has a frequency of 6000, then C = 6000, and rank 2 has about 3000, rank 3 about 2000, and rank 5 about 1200. This means the product of rank and frequency is roughly constant.

The two laws resemble each other in being distributions with a long tail and a high head. A very small number of items (prolific authors, top-ranked words) account for a large share, and the great majority appear rarely. So looking only at the average misreads the reality. Even in a field where the average number of papers is 1.5, some authors write dozens.

Let us see how they are used in library and information science. Zipf's law tells us that a few top words (particles, conjunctions) appear in most documents, so such words are regarded as having low discriminating power in retrieval, and their weights are lowered (the idf of an earlier lesson) or they are excluded from the index. Lotka's law is used to gauge the size of the core group of authors in a field or to compare output against the number of researchers.

Let us make the limits clear. The exponent of the law (the 2 in Lotka's law) varies with the field, the period, and the way of counting. If an exponent smaller than 2 appears in real data, it means there are more prolific authors. With a small sample the regularity does not show well, and results change with the counting criterion (all authors or first authors only). Finally, these laws only describe the observed distribution and do not explain why such a distribution arises.

examples.title: Building a Lotka prediction table
body: Conditions (a fictional field): 400 authors wrote only one paper. Apply Lotka's law (exponent 2).
Step 1: For n = 2, 400/2² = 100 authors; for n = 3, 400/3² ≈ 44 authors; for n = 4, 400/4² = 25 authors.

Step 2: Convert to numbers of papers. The 100 authors who wrote two papers wrote 100 × 2 = 200 papers in all, and the 25 authors who wrote four papers wrote 25 × 4 = 100 papers. Interpretation: the number of authors falls sharply, but the number of papers by prolific authors does not fall as much, so the share of a few authors is large.

examples.title: Comparing a Zipf frequency table with observations
body: Conditions (a fictional text collection): Assume the rank 1 word has a frequency of 6000 and follows Zipf's law.
Step 1: Since C = 6000, rank 2 is expected at 3000, rank 3 at 2000, rank 4 at 1500, and rank 5 at 1200. The sum of the top three words is 6000 + 3000 + 2000 = 11000.

Step 2: If rank 4 was observed at 1800, that is 20% more than the predicted 1500. Interpretation: the law is a rough outline, so it can be off at individual ranks, and if the deviation is large, one suspects that the exponent is not 1.

lis-14.title: Laws of Bibliometrics II: Bradford and the Scattering of Journals
explain: A library subscribes to journals to support astronomy research. In which journals do astronomy papers appear? It seems they would appear only in specialist astronomy journals, but in fact they are also scattered across physics, engineering, and earth science journals. Then must the library subscribe to all journals, or would a small number suffice? The regularity that answers this question is **Bradford's law**.

The British bibliographer Bradford, in the first half of the twentieth century, lined up the journals that carried papers on a subject in order of the number of papers on that subject. He then divided them into several zones so that the numbers of papers were similar, and found that the number of journals filling each zone grows by a constant multiple.

Written as steps, the procedure is as follows. Gather all the journals that carried papers related to the subject. Count the related papers in each journal. Rank them in order of the number of papers. Draw a line wherever the cumulative number of papers reaches one third of the total, dividing them into three zones. Then zone 1 holds a small number of highly productive journals (the core), zone 2 a medium number of journals, and zone 3 a large number of journals that carry only one or two papers each.

explain.alt: Three rows of bars. The left bar is the number of papers, and all three zones have the same length, "100 papers." The right bar is the number of journals: zone 1 has 5, zone 2 has 25, and zone 3 has 125, and the length grows progressively. Below is written "Each zone has the same number of papers, and journals increase as the rank goes down."

explain: The figure is this result. All three zones have the same 100 papers, but the journals increase to 5, 25, and 125. The ratio of the numbers of journals in neighboring zones is constant: 25/5 = 5 and 125/25 = 5. If this constant multiple is called n, the ratio of the numbers of journals in the zones can be written as follows. $$1 : n : n^2$$ 핵심 구역의 학술지 수를 $a$라 하면 세 구역은 $a$, $an$, $an^2$종이고 전체는 $a(1 + n + n^2)$종이다. (In English: if the number of journals in the core zone is a, the three zones have a, an, and an^2 journals, and the total is a(1 + n + n^2) journals.)

Let us do a calculation. If the core zone has 3 journals and n = 4, zone 2 has 3 × 4 = 12 journals and zone 3 has 3 × 16 = 48 journals, so the total number of journals is 3 + 12 + 48 = 63. One third of the papers are in 3 journals, but 60 more are needed to obtain the remaining two thirds. This asymmetry is the key implication of the law.

Libraries use this in their collection policy. If they subscribe first to the journals in the core zone, they can secure a considerable share of the literature at low cost, and for the journals in zone 3 they consider supplementing by interlibrary loan or by purchasing individual articles. Conversely, if a researcher must survey the subject without omission, search databases that find the scattered literature become important.

There are limits as well. The core zone is determined only by how many papers on the subject a journal carried, and does not mean the quality of the journal. The zones change depending on how the scope of the subject is set, and a newly emerged interdisciplinary subject may not fit the law well. Even a journal in zone 3 may have one or two articles that a particular researcher absolutely needs, so a decision to cancel subscriptions cannot be made on this law alone.

examples.title: Finding the zone multiple
body: Conditions: The three zones in the figure (5, 25, and 125 journals).
Step 1: Find the ratios of neighboring zones. Zone 2 / zone 1 = 25/5 = 5, and zone 3 / zone 2 = 125/25 = 5.

Step 2: Since the ratios are equal, n = 5 and the structure is 1 : 5 : 25. The total number of journals is 5 + 25 + 125 = 155, and the papers number 300. Interpretation: the top 5 journals (about 3% of the total) hold one third of the papers.

examples.title: A subscription policy scenario
body: Conditions (fictional): For the research subject of a university library there are 63 related journals (a 1 : 4 : 16 structure with 3 core journals), and the budget corresponds to 12 journals.

Step 1: The 3 core journals plus the 12 of zone 2 total 15, which exceeds the budget (12), so the library subscribes to all 3 core journals and picks 9 from zone 2. Step 2: The rest are supplemented by interlibrary loan. Interpretation: the 3 core journals are the baseline that secures one third of the papers, and in choosing from zone 2 the library also looks at users' needs and usage statistics.

lis-15.title: Citation Analysis: Bibliographic Coupling, Co-citation, and the h-index
explain: Papers cite earlier research in their references. Gathering these citation relations makes a map showing how papers are connected to one another. **Citation analysis** gauges, by the counts of these relations, which paper has great influence and which studies deal with the same subject. This lesson deals with concepts and calculations, and keeps in mind to the end that the numbers do not directly measure the value of research.

The simplest indicator is the number of times a paper has been cited by other papers. A much-cited paper is a sign that it has been widely read and consulted. But the number of citations alone does not show relations between papers. So two methods are used to measure how close two papers are.

- **Bibliographic coupling**: the degree to which two papers **cite the same references in common**. The number of shared references is the coupling strength
- **Co-citation**: the degree to which two papers are **cited together**. The number of later papers that cite both of these papers is the co-citation strength

It is important that the directions differ. Bibliographic coupling is fixed at the moment a paper is published, by its reference list, and does not change afterward. Co-citation changes in value as later papers accumulate over time. So bibliographic coupling is advantageous for grasping the field of a new paper right away, and co-citation for seeing the intellectual structure that has been recognized over time.

Let us see a calculation example. If the references of two new papers are N1 = {A, B, C, D, E} and N2 = {C, D, E, F}, the shared references are the three papers C, D, and E, so the bibliographic coupling strength is 3. Conversely, if the references of four later papers are Z1 = {X, Y, W}, Z2 = {X, V}, Z3 = {X, Y}, and Z4 = {Y, W}, the papers that cite X and Y together are Z1 and Z3, so the co-citation strength is 2.

The **h-index** is an indicator that tries to summarize an individual researcher's productivity and influence in one number. When a researcher's papers are lined up in order of the most citations, the h-index is the largest h such that the paper at rank h has h or more citations. That is, there are h papers each cited h or more times.

explain.alt: A bar chart. The horizontal axis is the paper rank (in order of most citations), 1 to 7, and the vertical axis is the number of citations. The numbers of citations of the bars from rank 1 are 12, 9, 7, 4, 4, 2, 1 in order. An orange dotted line is the diagonal representing "citations = rank."

explain: Let us read the figure. Count up to the place where the bars are above or touch the dotted line (citations = rank). The 12 citations at rank 1, 9 at rank 2, 7 at rank 3, and 4 at rank 4 are all at least the rank. Rank 5 has 4, which falls short of 5. So h = 4. A feature of the h-index is that even a single much-cited paper (12 citations) hardly affects the index.

There are many limits. Citation culture differs by field, so the h-indexes of mathematics and medicine cannot be compared directly, a longer career is an advantage, and the index can be inflated by self-citation or group citation. Even with the same h-index, a researcher whose citations are concentrated and one whose citations are evenly distributed are different in character. Because papers are also cited in order to criticize them, a citation is not necessarily a positive evaluation. So bibliometric indicators are used as material that supports human evaluation and cannot replace it.

examples.title: Computing bibliographic coupling and co-citation
body: Conditions (fictional): The references of new paper N1 are A, B, C, D, E, and the references of new paper N3 are B, C, G.

Step 1: Find the items that overlap in the two lists. B and C overlap. Step 2: Count them. The bibliographic coupling strength is 2. Interpretation: N1 and N3 share two earlier studies, so they may deal with the same subject, but that is only a possibility, not a certainty.

body: Conditions: The citation counts of one researcher's 5 papers are 10, 8, 5, 3, 2.
Step 1: Rank them in order of the most citations and compare with the rank. 1st: 10 ≥ 1, 2nd: 8 ≥ 2, 3rd: 5 ≥ 3, 4th: 3 ≥ 4 is false.
Step 2: The last rank at which it is true is h. h = 3. Interpretation: even if the most cited paper changes to 100 citations, h stays 3. The influence of that paper is hardly reflected in the index.

lis-16.title: Collection Development and Evaluation
explain: A library's budget and shelves are limited, and far more materials are published in a year than it can hold. So a systematic process is needed to decide which materials to buy, which to keep for a long time, and which to remove. This process is called **collection development**. The libraries and numbers in this lesson are all fictional, and do not describe the policies or regulations of any real library.

The philosophical basis for such judgments is Ranganathan's five laws of library science. (1) Books are for use. (2) Every reader his or her book. (3) Every book its reader. (4) Save the time of the reader. (5) The library is a growing organism. These sentences are less rules than standards to look back on when designing collections and services. Law 1 asks for use over mere holding, and law 5 asks for the renewal of the collection.

Collection development is a cycle. First one analyzes the user community to grasp its needs, **selects** materials according to policy, **acquires** them by purchase or donation, organizes and provides them, then **evaluates** use, and **weeds** materials that are worn out or unused. The evaluation results become the basis of the next selection, and the cycle goes round.

Numbers are used in evaluation. A representative indicator is the **collection turnover rate**. It is the number of loans in a year divided by the number of volumes held. If the library holds 12,000 volumes and has 18,000 loans in a year, the turnover rate is 18000 / 12000 = 1.5. Computing it by shelf zone lets one compare which areas are active and which are sleeping. When allocating a budget, the share of loans by zone is sometimes consulted. If total loans are 15,000 and literature has 4,500, the share of literature is 4500/15000 = 30%, so with a purchase budget of 20 million won, 6 million won is allocated to literature in proportion.

Weeding is the most delicate step. A widely introduced framework for weeding criteria is MUSTIE. The letters stand for Misleading content, Ugly (damaged condition), Superseded by a new edition, Trivial content, Irrelevant to the collection, and Elsewhere (easily available from another place). For example, an old practical book for which a revised edition has appeared falls under Superseded. This framework is a list of questions to examine, not an automatic scorecard.

Indicators must always be read together with context. A low turnover rate does not allow us to conclude that something has no value. Local history materials, rare materials, and reference books have a value only the library has, even with few loans. Conversely, an area with a high turnover rate means user demand is great, but pouring the budget into that area may cause materials for a minority of users to disappear. Laws 2 and 3 ask for this balance.

A collection, being a public resource, also carries the responsibility to guard against bias. If it leans toward the taste of the selectors or toward easy sources of purchase, the materials of a particular viewpoint or group go missing. This is the reason to reflect criteria other than loans (user surveys, community needs, diversity) and to make the policy public in writing.

examples.title: Comparing turnover rates
body: Conditions (a fictional library): 12,000 volumes held, 18,000 loans per year. Of these, the science zone has 2,000 volumes and 1,000 loans per year.

Step 1: The overall turnover rate is 18000/12000 = 1.5, and the science zone's is 1000/2000 = 0.5. Step 2: Compare. The science zone is at one third of the overall level. Interpretation: rather than shrinking the science zone on this number alone, first check the age of the materials, the user groups, and the way they are presented to users.

examples.title: Proportional budget allocation
body: Conditions: A purchase budget of 20 million won; the shares of loans by zone are literature 30%, social sciences 25%, science 15%, and other 30%.
Step 1: Compute the proportional allocation. Literature 6 million won, social sciences 5 million won, science 3 million won, and other 6 million won.

Step 2: Adjust. If the reason for the science zone's low turnover rate is old materials, consider taking part of the proportional allocation to spend more on renewing science materials. Interpretation: proportional allocation is only a starting point and is adjusted according to policy goals.

lis-17.title: Information Services and Access: Reference Service, Interlibrary Loan, and Open Access
explain: Even if the materials exist, a collection means nothing if users cannot find and use them. Libraries provide services that connect materials with users, and the most representative is **reference service**, in which a librarian answers users' questions and helps them find information. This lesson deals with general principles, and actual service regulations and copyright regulations differ by country and institution.

The question a user first asks often differs from the real information need. The question "Do you have books on bicycles?" might be about repair, about road traffic rules, or about a bicycle travelogue. So a **reference interview** is needed. The librarian listens to the user to the end, confirms what is really needed with open questions, builds and carries out a search strategy, provides the results, and follows up to check whether the user is satisfied. The key is not to interpret the question hastily.

Materials not held are obtained through **interlibrary loan**. It is a cooperative service of borrowing materials held by another library or receiving copies. It is a device that costs users almost nothing while sparing a library from having to buy every material. However, there is a processing cost per request and delivery takes time.

In scholarly information there is an access approach called **open access** (OA). It makes works publicly available so that anyone can read them without a subscription fee. It is commonly distinguished that **gold OA** is the approach in which a paper is open in the journal from the start, and **green OA** is the approach in which the author posts the manuscript to an institutional repository or the like to make it open. Which approach is possible depends on the journal, the contract, and copyright terms, so it is hard to generalize here.

Service decisions come with cost calculations. If the annual subscription fee for a bundle of journals is 12 million won and 4,000 articles were downloaded in a year, the **cost per use** is 12000000 / 4000 = 3,000 won. Suppose the cost of getting the same article by interlibrary loan is 8,000 won per item. The number of uses at which the costs of subscription and interlibrary loan become equal, the break-even point, is 12000000 / 8000 = 1,500 uses. If used more than 1,500 times, the subscription is cheaper; if less, interlibrary loan is cheaper. The current 4,000 is well above the break-even point, so the subscription is economical.

Such calculations are also dangerous if used without context. A journal with few uses may be essential to a small number of researchers, and usage statistics capture only use that took place within the library, not use that was never even attempted because access was difficult. Also, when collecting usage records to improve services, personal information must be collected at a minimum and the purpose made known, and libraries make protecting users' reading records a core of their ethics.

Fostering **information literacy** is also an extension of service. It helps users through user education in a sequence of abilities: noticing an information need, searching, evaluating, and using ethically. The building of search statements and the evaluation of sources learned in earlier lessons are all material for this education.

examples.title: Cost per use and break-even
body: Conditions (fictional): The annual subscription fee for a bundle of journals is 9 million won, annual use is 3,000, and interlibrary loan costs 6,000 won per item.

Step 1: The cost per use is 9000000 / 3000 = 3,000 won. Step 2: The break-even point is 9000000 / 6000 = 1,500 uses. Interpretation: with 3,000 uses, twice the break-even point, the subscription is economical, but if use falls to 1,000, interlibrary loan becomes cheaper.

Step 1: Rather than guiding the user straight to the shelf, the librarian asks an open question. "What will you use them for?" The user answers that it is for a middle school presentation. Step 2: Now that the need is clear, the librarian builds a search strategy centered on introductory books for young people and materials from trustworthy institutions. After providing the results, the librarian checks whether anything is lacking. Interpretation: even the same question calls for a different depth of material depending on the purpose.

lis-18.title: Records Management and Digital Preservation: Provenance and OAIS
explain: The materials dealt with so far were largely objects classified by subject, like books. But **records**, such as documents, ledgers, and photographs produced by an institution in the course of its work, are different in character. A record is evidence that proves what was done, when, and how, and it has meaning within the context of the work regardless of subject. The discipline that deals with such records is **records management** (archival science).

The two basic principles of records management are the **principle of provenance** and **respect for original order**. The principle of provenance is to manage records grouped by the institution or individual that created them, and not to mix them with records of other origins. Respect for original order is to maintain, as far as possible, the arrangement and order the records had when they were produced. Rearranging books by subject makes the shelves convenient, but rearranging records by subject erases the evidence of in which work process and in what order they were made.

Records are described at several levels. ISAD(G), an international description standard, has records described in a multilevel structure that descends from the largest unit, the fonds, through the series and the file to the item. Because the description of the upper level carries down to the lower level, even when looking at a single item, one can trace upward to which work of which institution it came from. Records also have a life cycle: through creation, use, and appraisal, they are divided into those to be kept permanently and those to be destroyed.

Electronic records and digital materials face risks different from paper. Storage media age and become unreadable, and file formats or programs disappear so that files cannot be opened. The international reference model that responds to this problem is **OAIS** (Open Archival Information System). The model explains the flow in which an archive receives, preserves, and provides information, using three kinds of **information packages**.

- **SIP** (Submission Information Package): the bundle the producer submits to the archive
- **AIP** (Archival Information Package): the bundle the archive preserves for the long term. It holds, together with the content, the information needed for preservation
- **DIP** (Dissemination Information Package): the bundle provided to users

explain.alt: From the box "Producer" on the left, an arrow labeled "SIP" enters the border of "Archive." Inside the archive, boxes "Ingest," "Archival storage (AIP held)," and "Access" are connected by arrows from top to bottom. From the "Access" box, an arrow labeled "DIP" goes out to the box "User" on the right.

explain: Let us follow the figure. When the producer sends a SIP, the archive first checks format and quality in the **ingest** stage and converts it into an AIP. The AIP is held in **archival storage**, and when a user makes a request, the **access** stage creates a DIP from the AIP and sends it out. The actual model also includes functions such as data management, administration, and preservation planning, but this figure shows only the core flow.

There are several methods in the practice of preservation. They are integrity checks that periodically compare **checksums** to see whether the contents of a file have not changed, replication that places the same AIP in several places, migration that moves old formats to new formats, and emulation that imitates the old environment. Replication increases capacity. If 500 AIPs are 4 GB each and 3 copies are kept, 500 × 4 × 3 = 6000 GB, that is, 6 TB, is needed (calculating 1 TB = 1000 GB).

There are limits and issues. Preservation keeps costing money. Format migration risks changing the look or function of the original, and emulation costs a great deal to implement the environment. Appraising what to preserve is a value judgment and so is accompanied by debate, and records containing personal information need a balance between openness and protection. This lesson deals with general principles, and actual legal obligations differ by country.

examples.title: A rearrangement that violates provenance
body: Conditions (a fictional institution): There are case files made by the welfare division of a fictional city hall. One file holds, in the order of handling, the petitions the welfare division received in 2010 and the results of handling them.

Step 1: Someone proposed organizing by subject and split the petitions into several files by their content. Step 2: The order of handling and the approval process of a single case were scattered, so it could no longer be confirmed which matter was handled in what order. Interpretation: finding by subject became easier, but the evidential value of the records was damaged. If subject access is needed, keep the original arrangement and build an index or search tool separately.

examples.title: Computing preservation capacity
body: Conditions: 800 AIPs, 2 GB each, 3 copies (1 TB = 1000 GB).

Step 1: The capacity of one copy is 800 × 2 = 1600 GB. Step 2: For 3 copies it is 1600 × 3 = 4800 GB = 4.8 TB. Interpretation: increasing the number of replicas makes the archive more resilient to disasters, but capacity and cost increase in proportion, so the number of replicas is set according to importance.

lis-19.title: Integrated Problem Solving: A Fictional Village Library Project
explain: The tools learned one by one so far are used together in real problems. Suppose the fictional Beodeul Village Library faces all of the problems below at once. Classification and cataloging decide where books are placed, retrieval decides how users find them, bibliometrics decides what to buy, and records management decides what to preserve for a long time and how. This lesson is practice in choosing which tool to use for which problem and in calculating.

The first step in solving a problem is diagnosis. If a user searches for "bird" and records written as "avian" do not come up, this is not a problem of the retrieval model but a problem of terminology. A concept has several names, so it is solved with a controlled vocabulary and cross-references (links between synonyms). Conversely, if there are too many results and the order is jumbled, it is not a terminology problem but a problem of the weighting model. Even with the same symptom, if the cause differs, the prescription differs.

Measures to raise retrieval performance move precision and recall together. Adding an AND condition to a query shrinks the results and tends to raise precision, but it may filter out even relevant documents and lower recall. So compute both P and R before and after the measure, and look at the overall effect with F1, which combines them. Judging by one indicator alone leads into a trap.

Weight calculation is turning the discriminating power of words into scores. A document's score is obtained by multiplying tf and idf for each word of the query and adding them. A common word has an idf near 0 and hardly affects the score. Therefore, adding needlessly common words to a query will not change the ranking.

Problems of collections and records require the ability to read indicators. In subscription decisions for journals, one looks at Bradford's zones and cost per use together. In evaluating researchers, one knows that the h-index is sensitive to the number of papers and to evenly distributed citations. To a proposal to rearrange local records by subject, one answers with the principle of provenance. No tool is all-powerful, and only when you can state its range of application and its limits can you be said to know how to use it.

When solving an integrated problem, keep to the order. (1) Summarize the problem in one sentence. (2) List candidate causes of the symptom. (3) Choose the tool and calculation that fit each candidate. (4) Interpret the calculation result and add its limits. We practice this order in the examples and questions below.

examples.title: The effect of adjusting a search statement
body: Conditions (fictional): The Beodeul Village Library catalog has 30 relevant documents. The first search returned 40 documents, of which 24 are relevant. After adding an AND condition, 25 documents come up, of which 20 are relevant.

Step 1: At first, P = 24/40 = 0.6, R = 24/30 = 0.8, and F1 = 2 × 0.6 × 0.8 / 1.4 ≈ 0.686. Step 2: After the adjustment, P = 20/25 = 0.8, R = 20/30 ≈ 0.667, and F1 = 2 × 0.8 × 0.667 / 1.467 ≈ 0.727. Interpretation: precision rose greatly and recall fell. F1 rose a little, so overall it is an improvement, but for a survey where recall matters, caution is needed.

examples.title: Summing query scores
body: Conditions: 5,000 documents. Among the three words of the query, A has df = 50 and appears 4 times in the document, B has df = 5000 and appears 20 times, and C has df = 500 and appears 3 times (base-10 logarithm).

Step 1: Find idf. A is log10(100) = 2, B is log10(1) = 0, and C is log10(10) = 1. Step 2: Multiply by tf and add. 4 × 2 + 20 × 0 + 3 × 1 = 8 + 0 + 3 = 11. Interpretation: word B, which appears most often, contributes nothing to the score, and the rare word A makes most of the score.

lis-20.title: Bachelor's Capstone: Designing Knowledge Organization and Retrieval for a Village Archive
explain: A capstone is an assignment of weaving the tools you have learned into one design, then explaining and verifying it. The fictional situation is as follows. The Yeoul Village Culture Archive has just digitized about 3,000 items of photographs, letters, workshop tool drawings, and event records that village residents had collected. The users are residents, students, and local researchers, and you, the library staff member, must design the classification, metadata, retrieval, and preservation plan. All materials and people are fictional.

First, diagnose the nature of the collection. This collection is not books but a mixture of records and photographs produced in the village. Instead of rearranging by subject, it must be made findable by subject while the provenance (which family or which group produced it) is kept. So set the principle of dividing the structure of preservation by the principle of provenance and the structure of finding by a separate retrieval tool.

Second, design the access structure. Users look for "what, where, and when." This can be divided naturally into facets. For example, if terms are fixed for four facets, object (photograph, letter, drawing), subject (workshop, marketplace, school), place (zones within the village), and period (by decade), filter search becomes possible. If the facets have 5, 4, 3, and 6 terms, there are 18 terms to define, and the possible combinations are 5 × 4 × 3 × 6 = 360. There is no need to write every single combination in the classification scheme in advance.

Third, design the metadata. Decide the core elements to put in all items (title, creator, date, subject terms, format, rights terms), and add elements by type of item (the recipient of a letter, the scale of a drawing). Manage subject terms with a controlled vocabulary so that when one concept has several names, like "marketplace" and "market," they gather into one. From the FRBR viewpoint, also decide how the same photograph issued in print and as a scan are related.

Fourth, design and evaluate retrieval. Use an inverted index and morphological analysis, and decide the scoring model. For evaluation, choose ten representative queries, have people judge in advance which items are relevant to each, and then compute the precision and recall of the system's results. For example, if in one query there are 70 relevant items, the system returned 50, and 35 of them are relevant, then P = 35/50 = 0.7 and R = 35/70 = 0.5. Since recall is low, consider increasing the links between synonyms.

Fifth, design preservation and ethics. For digital materials, follow the OAIS flow of receiving a SIP, holding it as an AIP, and providing a DIP to users. Check periodically with checksums and keep copies in several places. For letters or photographs containing personal information, the extent of openness must be set, and on copyright and portrait issues one gives only general principles and leaves specific judgments to the regulations of the institution concerned and to experts. Also state honestly the limits of the design (for example, that people cannot judge every item).

Finally, use bibliometric indicators as a supplement. Gather usage statistics to see which materials and facets are used often, and track over the long term how many times local research papers have cited this collection. However, indicators are only material for improving the design and do not prove the legitimacy of the design. After checking the key points with the questions below, write your own design in the final assignment.

examples.title: A sample design: facets and metadata
body: Conditions (part of the fictional collection): "Autumn 1998 Marketplace Photo" is a photograph taken at the village marketplace, its location is the central zone of the village, and its period is the 1990s.

Step 1: Assign to facets. The object is a photograph, the subject is the marketplace, the place is the central zone of the village, and the period is the 1990s. Step 2: Fill in the metadata. The title is as above, the creator is unknown, the date is autumn 1998, the subject term is the controlled vocabulary term "marketplace" (linked from the similar word "market"), and the rights terms are under review. Interpretation: elements that are not known are not left blank but recorded as "unknown" or "under review," so that the next staff member can carry on.

examples.title: A sample verification: when recall is low
body: Conditions: In the query "marketplace photograph," there are 70 relevant items, the system result is 50, and 35 of them are relevant.

Step 1: Find P = 35/50 = 0.7 and R = 35/70 = 0.5. Step 2: Looking at the 35 missed items, a considerable number have only "market" written. Add a link "market → marketplace" to the controlled vocabulary and evaluate again. Interpretation: the cause was a terminology mismatch, not the scoring function, so linking synonyms comes before adjusting the weights.
